concept.name: Married put
concept.definition: A married put is a protective put in which the underlying shares and the put option are purchased simultaneously as a single package, rather than the put being added to a pre-existing stock holding. The put guarantees a minimum sale price for the shares until expiration.
concept.intuition: It is buying a stock and its insurance policy on the same ticket — you know your maximum possible loss on the combined position from day one.
concept.mechanics: Buy 100 shares and one put at the same time. The payoff is identical to a protective put; the distinction is transactional (simultaneous purchase, which also matters for tax-lot identification in some jurisdictions). By put-call parity the position is equivalent to a long call plus discounted strike cash.
concept.formula: Maximum loss = (S_0 - K) + premium, per share; profit = max(S_T, K) - S_0 - premium.
concept.failure_modes: Same as protective puts: the recurring premium drag compounds over time, and protection ends at expiration. Choosing strikes too far OTM leaves a large deductible; too far ITM makes the 'insurance' cost prohibitive.
concept.misconceptions: A married put is not a distinct payoff from a protective put — many texts use the terms interchangeably; the only real difference is the timing of the stock and put purchases. It does not make a falling-stock position safe, only loss-limited.
concept.example: Buy 100 shares of XYZ at $50 and simultaneously buy the $50 put for $2.50. Worst case at expiration is a $250 loss; if XYZ rises to $60 the net gain is ($10 - $2.50) x 100 = $750.
